answer: About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs left or were driven from their homes in 1947 to 1949; Britannica gives a range of 520,000 to 1,000,000 and says the number likely exceeded 700,000, and Benny Morris says 700,000. Morris describes expulsions from Lydda and Ramle in July 1948, where he counts 50,000 to 60,000 people driven out, and says most other refugees fled out of fear of the war. Historians disagree on the weight of each cause. Morris says there was no master plan but that expulsion was real; Khalidi calls it expulsion and Pappe calls it ethnic cleansing and says it was planned; Efraim Karsh puts most blame on Arab leaders. In some places, such as Haifa, local Arab leaders ordered or advised leaving. Our reading: a fair answer does not deny expulsions and does not say they were the only cause.

contested: Causes: Morris (war, fear and some expulsions, no master plan; in the same article he also writes of 'partial ethnic cleansing' and calls the expulsions 'inevitable' and sensible, a moral view this card does not adopt), Khalidi (expulsion, 'three-quarters of a million'; the cited pages do not use the phrase ethnic cleansing for him), Pappe (planned ethnic cleansing under Plan Dalet), Karsh (mainly Arab leadership failure; he disputes Morris's reading of the documents).

Numbers: 520,000 to 1,000,000 is Britannica's range; the UN's 1949-50 figure (just over 700,000) is reported through a summary of Morris's talk. Relief counts are lower because they count people needing aid.
Whether Lydda and Ramle were expelled on a top-down order: Morris in his article says soldiers were ordered to empty the towns; other writers dispute how far the order went.

Calls to leave: local leaders ordering departures (Haifa) are in Karsh and in the summary of Morris's talk. A general radio order is argued against by Erskine Childers, as reported by MERIP, a source labelled advocacy here.
could_not_verify: A readable page with Erskine Childers's 1961 finding on Arab radio broadcasts, other than MERIP (advocacy). Not counted.
Pappe's 2006 Journal of Palestine Studies article: the PDF did not load. His own words are taken from an interview and an Al Jazeera quotation.
Morris's 1988 book The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem: no readable page. His own words come from a 2004 Los Angeles Times article reprinted by HNN, and a conference summary.
A third reliable source for the early departure of wealthier families (two used).
The UN Conciliation Commission's own 1949-50 count: I found it only through the Israel Law Review summary.
Primary documents for the Lydda and Ramle order (Rabin and Ben-Gurion diaries): no readable page.
not_claimed: This card does not deny that expulsions happened. It says they happened in specific places.
It does not claim all 700,000 were expelled, or that all fled voluntarily.
It does not claim the Arab radio-orders story is proven; the evidence on it is thin and disputed.
It does not address the right of return, property, or who is responsible for the refugees' present status.

answer_claims.says: About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs left or were driven from their homes in 1947 to 1949; Britannica gives a range of 520,000 to 1,000,000 and says the number likely exceeded 700,000, and Benny Morris says 700,000.
Morris describes expulsions from Lydda and Ramle in July 1948, where he counts 50,000 to 60,000 people driven out, and says most other refugees fled out of fear of the war.
Historians disagree on the weight of each cause.
Morris says there was no master plan but that expulsion was real; Khalidi calls it expulsion and Pappe calls it ethnic cleansing and says it was planned; Efraim Karsh puts most blame on Arab leaders.
In some places, such as Haifa, local Arab leaders ordered or advised leaving.
Our reading: a fair answer does not deny expulsions and does not say they were the only cause.

skeptic.notes: Read two or more sources per fact. Pro-Palestinian attack (the stronger one): the card leans on Benny Morris through two doors (his 2004 article and a conference summary in the Israel Law Review) and so 'most fled out of fear' (fact 3), 'elite left first' (fact 4), the UN 700,000 figure and the Haifa order (fact 5) are one historian counted twice; the second voice is Karsh, who is on the other side. No Palestinian historian is quoted on cause except in heard. The Israel Law Review also reports a fourth stage (October-November 1948, about 200,000 more refugees after IDF offensives) that the card leaves out, and Morris's own article calls it 'partial ethnic cleansing', which the answer hid by crediting that phrase to Khalidi and Pappe. Pro-Israel attack: the answer opens with Lydda and Ramle and never says the Arab states' invasion and the civil war after November 1947 are the setting; the Haifa evidence is Karsh and a Morris summary against Childers via an advocacy source, and the page says Morris found no policy by Arab leaders to order flight. must-fix (done): fact 1 cited the Israel Law Review for 'about 500,000', but that line is about people moved within Palestine, not the UNRWA relief count; source removed, fact now has two reliable sources. must-fix (done): Khalidi was said to use the term ethnic cleansing; his cited pages say 'expelled'. should-fix: Morris counted twice - add an independent third source for facts 3 and 4 (Palestinian-side scholar). should-fix: add a fact on the autumn 1948 expulsions and on Israel's refusal of return, since heard names it. nit: the 'UN concluded just over 700,000' is a summary of a talk, so the answer no longer asserts it. Britannica pages read from the archive copy.

citer.notes: Reworded 'Historians agree expulsions happened in specific places, Lydda and Ramle being the clearest': Karsh does not say that, so 'agree' was unsupported; now attributed to Morris (facts 2, 3). Reworded 'Khalidi and Pappe call it ethnic cleansing' to separate them (fact 7 sources). Removed 'and the UN concluded just over 700,000' (only a summary of a talk carries it). Marked the last sentence 'Our reading'. All sentences tied in answer_claims. Holds for the answer as worded; skeptic verdict stays weakened.
